results.summary: This project implements a 12-bit PDP8 CPU core in Verilog, excluding the extended arithmetic unit so it lacks multiply and divide instructions. It communicates over a custom 5-clock bus interface that multiplexes 12-bit addresses and data through 8-bit pins, with separate phases for address, data, and I/O cycles. An assembler is included mainly for testing purposes, and testbench code is provided. The design is notable for being a compact reimplementation of a classic minicomputer architecture on a single Tiny Tapeout tile.

ChipTune is an 8-bit programmable sound generator that replicates vintage square-wave audio and outputs 4-bit DAC audio. It receives serial data via a UART interface at 300 baud, with control signals for address/data selection and mode. The design also includes a re-imagined scan controller (version 2) to demonstrate faster data acquisition, using a JTAG-like topology with a short register chain. External hardware needed includes a computer COM port for serial communication, and the design is notable for its dual purpose as both an audio device and a scan chain experiment.

This design is an 8-bit multiplier that processes two 8-bit numbers in 4-bit chunks (nibbles) over multiple clock cycles. It uses a valid signal to latch each nibble sequentially, and a toggle bit to select which half of the 16-bit result is output on the 8-bit output pins. The multiplication is performed in a bit-serial fashion, requiring several clock cycles per operation. The design is notable for its minimal interface and chunked processing approach.

This project implements a simple digital clock that displays the time of day on four 7-segment displays. It takes a clock input and outputs serial data to shift registers that drive the displays, using srclk, rclk, and ser signals. The design includes inputs for minutes and hours, likely for setting the time. It is a straightforward clock design intended for educational or basic timekeeping purposes.

This project is a two-bit universal finite state machine inspired by Rue Mohr's 1Bit CPU, implemented as a Moore FSM where the next-state logic is stored in a dual-port RAM. Instructions are loaded into the RAM via a 16-bit shift register using a specific serial format, and the FSM uses two input bits and two output bits. External hardware such as a microcomputer (e.g., Arduino) is required to load the RAM instructions, and a clock is needed to run the FSM. The design is notable for its flexible, programmable nature and educational value in demonstrating FSM concepts.

This is a guitar tuner design that measures the frequency of input pulses and displays the result on a 7-segment display. It uses a fixed window approach for frequency discrimination, dividing the clock and converting binary to decimal for display. The design requires external hardware to condition the analog input signal into clean digital pulses, as detailed in the Neptune project. It is notable for being part of the Neptune tuner series and includes a slower square wave output on one pin.

This is a guitar tuner design similar to the fixed window version but using a proportional window approach for frequency discrimination. It measures input pulse frequency and displays the result on a 7-segment display, with clock division and binary-to-decimal conversion. External hardware is needed to convert the analog input signal into clean digital pulses, as described in the Neptune project. The design is notable for its proportional window method, which may offer different accuracy characteristics.

This project implements a PWM controller to adjust LED brightness using two buttons for increasing and decreasing the duty cycle. It includes debouncing logic for the button inputs and outputs signals indicating when maximum or minimum duty cycle is reached, as well as a 1 Hz clock. The design operates from a 12.5 kHz clock and provides a PWM output that ranges from 0% to 100%. It is a simple experiment demonstrating PWM and button debouncing.

This project implements a Hamming(7,4) encoder and decoder for error correction. It has a mode pin to select between encoding (0) and decoding (1), with 4-bit input and 7-bit output in encode mode, and 7-bit input with 4-bit data plus error flag in decode mode. The design is purely combinational and can be tested using the provided Python test script. It is notable for providing a compact hardware implementation of a classic error-correcting code.

This project plays the song 'Bad Apple' through a piezo speaker connected across two output pins using differential PWM modulation. It converts an RTTL ringtone into Verilog and plays it back when a 12 kHz clock is provided and a reset pulse is applied. The design requires an external piezo speaker connected between io_out[0] and io_out[1]. It is notable for being a simple music player based on a previous Tiny Tapeout project.
